characters: Hawawu Shaibu: a 14-year-old girl in a school uniform and a headscarf, holding a notebook.
Hajia Asana: Hawawu’s grandmother, a farmer in a wrapper and headscarf, standing by sacks of maize.
Mr Tia: the agriculture teacher, in a work shirt, holding a printed research paper.
The storeroom: a dim room with sacks of maize on the floor and a few weevils crawling on a sack.

narrationPlan.voice: Determined girl’s voice for Hawawu; a warm, firm grandmother’s voice for Hajia Asana; a patient teacher’s voice for Mr Tia
narrationPlan.pace: Clear and practical, slowing for the figures (about 118 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Warm northern drum and a steady flute; a bright tune when the clean grain is opened (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Hawawu, Hajia Asana and Mr Tia are invented. The research facts come from a 2018 IFPRI working paper on the cost-effectiveness of post-harvest technologies in Ghana: causes of loss (insects, mould, early or late harvest, grain not dry enough, selling at harvest); hermetic bags kept maize dry-weight loss below an average of 0.5 per cent over six months, cost about GH¢9 (US$2) in 2018 and gave better returns in Tamale over eight months; typical cabbage losses of about 60 per cent in Ghana; a zero energy cool chamber trial raised the saleable share after six days from 40 to 62 per cent, cost about US$1,040 and paid back after 18 uses.

The paper’s figures for maize losses of 10 to 30 per cent in ordinary storage are not Ghana-specific, and the story says so. Prices are from 2018 and the story tells learners to check current prices. Sums in the story use invented numbers, labelled as imaginary.

The story does not claim that a bag solves price problems or replaces drying; it shows an elder who tests one bag first and keeps the grain dry. It gives no medical advice about aflatoxin beyond naming it.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Have an agricultural officer or post-harvest researcher check the descriptions of hermetic bags and the cool chamber, the 2018 figures and the dryness advice against current guidance.
Check the explanation of how a zero energy cool chamber keeps produce cool, because the paper’s summary gave results, not the mechanism.
Check the report-writing tip against the NaCCA English syllabus.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about reducing losses after harvest. It uses real trial figures with their dates and limits and models a short report.
learningGoals: Name two causes of post-harvest loss.
Explain how a hermetic bag protects grain and what the farmer must still do.
Write a short report with a heading, introduction, findings and recommendation.
beforeReading: Ask: where does food go between the farm and the plate? When can it be lost?
whileReading: At page 6, ask learners to say why the numbers are marked as imaginary.
afterReading: Write a report on how your family or school stores a food item.
Visit a market (with an adult) and ask how sellers keep vegetables fresh.
discussion: Why might a family sell grain cheaply right after harvest? What might help?
What might stop a family from buying a bag?
reflection: What food is wasted at home or at school, and how could it be saved?

mathsExtension.task: Suppose 100 kg of maize is worth GH¢300 and 20 per cent is lost. How much value is lost?
Suppose 0.5 per cent is lost instead. What is the loss in value?
A bag costs GH¢9 (2018 figure). How many bags can GH¢90 buy?

support: Provide a report frame: HEADING, Introduction (one sentence), Findings (two facts), Recommendation (one sentence), name and date.
stretch: Compare the cost and benefits of a bag and a metal silo using the paper’s figures (a 0.5-ton silo cost about US$200 in 2018) and write a recommendation with a reason.

localiseThis: Ask your district agricultural officer which storage methods suit the crops and climate in your area and where hermetic bags are sold; do not rely on 2018 prices.

factCheck.claim: Hermetic PICS bags kept maize dry-weight loss below an average of 0.5 per cent over six months, cost about GH¢9 (US$2) for a 50 to 100 kg bag in 2018 and gave better returns than other options over eight months in Tamale; typical cabbage losses in Ghana are about 60 per cent; a zero energy cool chamber trial raised the saleable share after six days from 40 to 62 per cent, cost about US$1,040 and paid back after 18 uses.
factCheck.explanation: From a 2018 IFPRI working paper; trial results and prices from that period.
factCheck.reference: Baral, S. and Hoffmann, V. (2018), “Tackling Post Harvest Loss in Ghana: Cost-Effectiveness of Technologies”, IFPRI Working Paper (cgspace.cgiar.org).

factCheck.claim: Causes of post-harvest loss include insects (maize weevil, larger grain borer), mould and aflatoxin, harvesting too early or late, grain not dry enough, and selling immediately after harvest, which one study linked to a loss equal to 29.3 per cent of grain sales value.
factCheck.explanation: From the same paper; the last figure is from a study the paper cites.

reviewerNotes: Confirm language of origin in northern Ghana context.
